extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, humor theory, literary critics, and researchers of jokes/humor
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and classifying the technical methods by which jokes are constructed (e.g., condensation, multiple use, double meaning, displacement) and the psychical processes underlying joke-work. Intended as guidance for analyzing why particular utterances function as jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke technique dominated by compression or saving of expression, realized (I) as (a) formation of composite word and (b) with modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include composite-word jokes and modifications that fuse two thoughts into one expression. Condensation is presented as the most general category under which many joke-techniques fall (multiple use and play upon words as special cases). Note the caveat: condensation/economy alone does not make a joke — there is a peculiar kind of abbreviation specific to jokes. Examples: Hamlet quote, name-play such as 'Leidenschaft - Eifersucht'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple use of the same material
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same verbal material in more than one sense or context (Group II: (c) as a whole and in parts, (d) in a different order, (e) with slight modification, (f) of the same words full and empty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes dividing up, re-arrangement, slight modification, or using words 'full' versus 'empty' (literal vs auxiliary). Play upon words is treated as the ideal case of multiple use. Examples: question-answer reuse (Saphir example), 'have you taken a bath?' where 'take' functions full vs empty. Reduction tests: changing order or wording often destroys the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning (polysemy and its subtypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a word/phrase that legitimately bears two meanings, producing a joke by switching or exploiting those meanings (Group III: (g) meaning as a name and as a thing, (h) metaphorical and literal meanings, (i) double meaning proper/play upon words, (j) double entendre, (k) double meaning with an allusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish subcases: play upon words where one word expresses both meanings; double entendre where sexual meaning is involved (sometimes hidden); double meaning with an allusion where one meaning is more prominent and the other lies behind it. Examples: 'innocence' (legal vs sexual), Spitzer’s wage/lie-back example, Heine’s obscenity-like line. Beware that unequal prominence of meanings leads to specific subtypes ('double meaning with an allusion').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to economy / compression (unifying principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general tendency across joke-techniques to 'save' expression — compressing or omitting an expected second thought because a single expression covers both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy explains why many techniques (condensation, multiple use, double meaning) create jokes: they avoid stating a second thought explicitly. Examples: 'C’est le premier vol de l’aigle' (flight/theft), 'Iron front - iron cash-box - Iron Crown'. Important warning: not every linguistic economy is a joke (laconic remarks are not automatically jokes); there must be a specific kind of abbreviation peculiar to jokes, and sometimes the intellectual effort required offsets the surface saving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns / Kalauer (sound-jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sub-species of verbal joke characterized by similarity of sound rather than exact identity of meaning; often regarded as the cheapest or lowest form of verbal joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include vowel changes, rhyme, shared initial letters, or assonance. Puns demand relatively little technical effort and are often considered inferior to true plays upon words. Examples and anti-examples: Heine’s Kalkutta/Kalkuttenbraten (criticized because words are actually identical in origin), Capuchin monk’s sermon examples. Fischer’s view (a pun plays upon sound, play upon words on meaning) is discussed but Freud treats puns as a sub-type of the broader play-upon-words group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement (diversion of the train of thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique where the reply or continuation diverts psychical emphasis from the thought suggested by the remark to a different, often subsidiary, thought — producing a joke by shifting standpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displacement is largely independent of verbal wording (depends on train of thought) and is best labeled where the joke-work itself performs the shift (not merely the hearer's interpretation). Examples: 'Salmon mayonnaise' anecdote (answering a reproach with a different logical interpretation), the bath-joke (accent shift from 'bath' to 'taken'), Heine's 'Golden Calf' retort. Displacement can combine with double meaning when wording admits an unintended secondary sense that enables the diversion. Reduction tests: undoing the displacement (i.e., making the respondent answer the intended reproach) destroys the joke and converts it into cynicism or a non-jokey reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on precise wording / form-dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes rely crucially on the exact phrasing or surface form; altering the wording can abolish the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jokes vanish if a particular phrase is replaced by an equivalent wording ('taken a bath' vs 'bathed'); other jokes (displacement-type) may be more independent of wording. Analytic method: use reductions by changing wording to test whether the joke's technique is lexical (double meaning/pun) or structural (displacement, rearrangement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement / reversal of relations (means and ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques that produce joke-effect by reversing or rearranging the logical relation between elements (for example reversing means and ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the drunk tutor who says he tutors in order to drink (reversal of means and ends) — the joke depends on this reversal and on its particular expression; reducing the expression to a plain statement of cynicism removes the joke. This is treated as a form of rearrangement within the multiple-use family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing jokes (illustrative/role-based jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that function to characterise a social type or individual's habitual traits (outer shell) while having a deeper technical mechanism behind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'Schadchen' (marriage-broker) who says 'You surely don’t call that living?' — superficially a character-revealing jest, but technically relying on double meaning ('living') and displacement. Analysts should distinguish the surface character portrayal from the underlying joke-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological distinction: joke-work (construction) vs understanding (reception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A methodological principle: do not confuse the psychical processes that construct the joke (joke-work) with those by which a listener understands it (reception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud insists the current enquiry is into joke-work (how jokes are built); similar-seeming processes (e.g., displacement vs double meaning) may play different roles in construction vs reception. Use reduction experiments to separate what is part of the joke's construction from what is merely a route for understanding it.
